culture.title: Kaomise Kabuki at the Minamiza
culture.description: Japan's oldest kabuki theatre runs its grand December season with the actors' names on painted boards above the entrance, which is the event of the Kyoto year.
culture.bonus: Rent the English audio guide and follow one actor's role all the way through.

culture.title: Nijo Castle's Nightingale Floors
culture.description: The shogun's Kyoto palace, where the corridor floors were built to chirp under any footstep so nobody could approach unheard.
culture.bonus: Try to cross one section of the floor silently. You cannot.

culture.title: Gion Corner's Hour of Seven Arts
culture.description: One sitting covering tea ceremony, koto, flower arranging, court music, kyogen comedy, puppet theatre and a maiko dance, which is the shortcut to all of it.
culture.bonus: Pick the one art you liked most and go and find a full-length performance of it.

culture.title: The Gekkeikan Okura Sake Museum
culture.description: A 1909 brewery warehouse in Fushimi showing how sake was made by hand, with the old cedar vats and tools in place and a tasting at the end.
culture.bonus: Taste the one bottle the museum only sells on site and nowhere else.

culture.title: Sanjusangendo's Thousand and One Kannon
culture.description: A hall 120 metres long holding 1,001 gilded wooden statues in ranks, carved in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, every face slightly different.
culture.bonus: Walk the full length looking for the one statue whose face resembles someone you know.

culture.title: Ryoan-ji's Fifteen Rocks from the Veranda
culture.description: The most famous dry garden in the world is fifteen rocks in raked gravel, arranged so that you can never see all fifteen from any one spot on the veranda.
culture.bonus: Try every position on the veranda and prove the fifteenth rock really is hidden.

culture.title: Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion
culture.description: Two floors covered in gold leaf standing in a reflecting pond, rebuilt in 1955 after a monk burned the original down, and worth the crowd exactly once.
culture.bonus: Go at opening time and get the reflection before the pond surface is disturbed.

culture.title: A Tea Ceremony at Camellia on Ninenzaka
culture.description: A forty-five-minute ceremony in a small teahouse on the stone lane below Kiyomizu-dera, explained in English, where you whisk your own bowl at the end.
culture.bonus: Eat the sweet before the tea, in the order you are told, and taste why.

8ball.title: Get Off at a Station You Have Never Heard Of
8ball.description: Take any local line out of the centre, ride past the stop you meant to use, get off somewhere with no listing in any guide, and spend the afternoon there.
8ball.bonus: Eat wherever has the most bicycles parked outside it.

8ball.title: Stay an Hour at the First Temple You Pass
8ball.description: Kyoto has sixteen hundred temples and you were going to see four of them. Walk out of wherever you are staying and give a full hour to the first one you reach.
8ball.bonus: Do not look up its name until the hour is over.

social.title: The Fushimi Sake District Tasting Walk
social.description: Forty breweries in one canal-side district south of the city, with black timber warehouses, willow-lined water, and tasting rooms a few minutes apart.
social.bonus: Taste the same grade of sake at two different breweries back to back and name the difference.

social.title: Sake Bar Yoramu's Eight-Seat Counter
social.description: An Israeli sake expert pouring aged and obscure bottles you will not find anywhere else, from a counter with almost no seats in it.
social.bonus: Take the tasting flight and let him choose all three without input.

social.title: A Karaoke Box Off Kawaramachi
social.description: Your own room, a tambourine nobody asked for, and drinks brought to the door until whatever hour you booked it to.
social.bonus: Sing something in Japanese off the on-screen phonetics with no idea what it means.

social.title: Bar K6's Whisky Wall
social.description: A long-standing Kiyamachi counter bar with a back wall of single malts and a bartender who will talk you through it if you ask properly.
social.bonus: Say what you normally drink and let the bar talk you out of it.

social.title: Hanamikoji After Dark, Main Street Only
social.description: Gion's lantern-lit main street at nine at night, with wooden ochaya fronts on both sides and the occasional geiko crossing between appointments.
social.bonus: Stay on the public street the whole time and get one photo of the lanterns, not of a person.

social.title: Whisky at Bar Rocking Chair
social.description: A dim counter bar off Kiyamachi built around Japanese whisky and properly made classics, with the unhurried pace Kyoto bartending is known for.
social.bonus: Order a Japanese whisky you have never seen on a shelf outside Japan.

social.title: Kyoto Beer Lab on the Takase Canal
social.description: A small brewery taproom beside the old canal doing beers brewed with matcha, hojicha and yuzu, which sounds gimmicky and is not.
social.bonus: Drink the tea-brewed beer before the normal one so you taste it properly.

social.title: Jazz on Vinyl in a Kyoto Kissa
social.description: A jazz kissa is a listening bar with a wall of records and a rule about not talking, built around a hi-fi somebody has spent decades on.
social.bonus: Sit through one full side of a record without saying a word.

social.title: Standing-Bar Hop Through Kiyamachi
social.description: The canal street parallel to Pontocho, where tachinomi standing bars charge by the glass and nobody expects you to stay for a second.
social.bonus: One drink per place, four places, and talk to someone in each.

social.title: Pontocho Alley, End to End
social.description: A lane barely two metres wide running five blocks between Shijo and Sanjo, packed on both sides with bars and restaurants stacked three storeys up.
social.bonus: Walk the entire alley once before picking anywhere, then go back to the third place you liked.

social.title: L'Escamoteur's Steampunk Attic
social.description: A magic-themed cocktail bar up a staircase in a narrow brick building, run by a French bartender who does sleight of hand across the counter.
social.bonus: Ask for a trick before you ask for a second drink.

social.title: Bee's Knees, Behind the Yellow Door
social.description: A Prohibition-era speakeasy in Gion disguised as a bookshop, where the only way in is through a bright yellow door and the cocktails are worth the theatre.
social.bonus: Order off the bartender's recommendation instead of the menu.

chill.title: The Botanical Gardens by the Kamo
chill.description: Japan's oldest public botanical garden, on the river in the north of the city, with a conservatory and a cherry grove and hardly a tourist in it.
chill.bonus: Find the oldest tree on the site and work out what year it was planted.

chill.title: The Kamo River Bank at Dusk
chill.description: Between Shijo and Sanjo the whole city comes down to sit on the grass in an evenly spaced row and watch the light go: students, couples, salarymen, buskers.
chill.bonus: Buy a canned drink from a konbini and join the row at the regulation spacing.

chill.title: Daisen-in's Gardens Inside Daitoku-ji
chill.description: One walled Zen monastery holds two dozen sub-temples, and this one's dry gardens are read as a river running from the mountains out to an ocean of raked gravel.
chill.bonus: Work out which garden is the mountains and which is the sea before reading the sign.

chill.title: Moss and Maples at Gio-ji
chill.description: A thatched hut and a carpet of moss at the quiet end of Arashiyama, built for a dancer who was abandoned by a warlord and became a nun.
chill.bonus: Sit on the step of the hut and stay until someone else arrives.

chill.title: The Open-Air Bath at Kurama Onsen
chill.description: A mountain hot spring at the end of the Eizan line where the outdoor pool sits in a cedar valley, and you reach it on the same trip as the Kurama hike.
chill.bonus: Soak after the hike over from Kibune, not before it.

chill.title: Shosei-en, the Garden Behind the Station
chill.description: A walled stroll garden with a pond and teahouses ten minutes from Kyoto Station, which almost everyone arriving in the city walks straight past.
chill.bonus: Go on your arrival day with your bag still in a locker and start the trip here.

chill.title: Weekenders Coffee in the Courtyard
chill.description: A tiny roastery hidden at the back of a car park in Nakagyo, in a restored machiya with a gravel garden and nowhere to sit but outside.
chill.bonus: Find it without checking the map more than once.

chill.title: % Arabica on the Katsura River
chill.description: A glass box of a coffee bar on the Arashiyama riverbank, with a queue by ten and a view straight up the valley if you get there before it.
chill.bonus: Take the cup to the Togetsukyo bridge and drink it looking back at the mountain.

chill.title: Funaoka Onsen's 1923 Tiled Bathhouse
chill.description: A neighbourhood sento from 1923 with carved wooden transom panels, a tiny outdoor rock bath, and an electric bath that nobody warns you about.
chill.bonus: Get in the denki-buro, the electric one, for at least five seconds.

chill.title: Kurasu, the Roaster by Kyoto Station
chill.description: A pared-back specialty bar a few minutes from the station, which makes it the right first or last hour of any Kyoto trip.
chill.bonus: Ask for the single origin on filter and drink it without sugar or milk.

foodie.title: Kizakura Kappa Country in Fushimi
foodie.description: A working sake brewery in the southern canal district with its own izakaya and a craft beer line, in a complex built around a water-goblin mascot.
foodie.bonus: Drink the unpasteurised sake that only ever gets poured on the brewery site.

foodie.title: Dinner on a Yuka Platform Over the Kamo
foodie.description: Every summer the Pontocho restaurants build wooden decks out over the river on stilts, and eating on one is the single most Kyoto thing available.
foodie.bonus: Book the platform rather than the indoor room, whatever the price difference.

foodie.title: Matcha and Wagashi at Ippodo's Kaboku Tearoom
foodie.description: A tearoom at the back of a tea merchant trading since 1717, where they bring the whisk and the bowl and let you make the matcha yourself.
foodie.bonus: Make your own bowl rather than ordering it served, and get the froth right.

foodie.title: Breakfast at Badu, Monk's Other Room
foodie.description: The Monk team's second place, opened in 2025, doing a smaller daytime menu out of the same obsession with one oven and local produce.
foodie.bonus: Go on a weekday morning and take whatever the single daily option is.

foodie.title: Eat at the Stall at Nishiki Market
foodie.description: Four hundred years of covered market in a lane five metres wide (tamagoyaki, pickles, soy milk doughnuts, grilled eel) eaten standing at the counter you bought it from.
foodie.bonus: Buy one thing you cannot identify and eat it before you ask what it was.

foodie.title: Wood-Fired Dinner at Monk
foodie.description: A twelve-seat room on the Philosopher's Path with one oven, one set menu, and a pizza that people book two months out to eat.
foodie.bonus: Do not ask what is coming next. Let the whole set menu land unannounced.

foodie.title: Kaiseki at Kikunoi Honten
foodie.description: Three generations of the Murata family running the most serious kaiseki house in Japan, where the meal is built entirely around what week of the year it is.
foodie.bonus: Ask which single ingredient on the menu will be gone in a fortnight, and why.

foodie.title: Counter Kaiseki at Giro Giro Hitoshina
foodie.description: A canal-side townhouse where young cooks in bandanas do a full kaiseki course at an open counter for a fraction of what the old houses charge.
foodie.bonus: Take a counter seat rather than a table and watch every plate get built.

foodie.title: Tempura Endo Yasaka in Gion
foodie.description: A Michelin-starred tempura house in a Gion townhouse, where each piece comes out of the oil onto your plate one at a time for two hours.
foodie.bonus: Eat every piece within ten seconds of it landing, which is the only correct way.

foodie.title: Burnt Miso Ramen at Kyoto Gogyo
foodie.description: They scorch the miso broth in a wok over an open flame until it goes black, which sounds like a mistake and tastes like the best idea anyone has had.
foodie.bonus: Order the burnt soy sauce version too and split both bowls with whoever you came with.

foodie.title: Omen's Udon by Ginkaku-ji
foodie.description: Thick cold noodles served with a bowl of broth and a plate of seven sesame-dressed vegetables you pile in yourself, at the end of the Philosopher's Path.
foodie.bonus: Put every vegetable in before you taste it, the way the counter tells you to.

foodie.title: Menya Inoichi Hanare's Dashi Ramen
foodie.description: A Michelin-listed shop that treats ramen broth like kaiseki stock, built from Rausu kombu and dried seafood instead of pork bones.
foodie.bonus: Drink the last of the broth straight from the bowl before you judge it.

adventure.title: The Nanzen-ji Aqueduct and the Keage Incline
adventure.description: A Meiji-era brick aqueduct running straight through the middle of a Zen temple, and the abandoned railway incline that used to haul canal boats up the hill.
adventure.bonus: Walk the disused rails of the incline from top to bottom on the sleepers.

adventure.title: The Philosopher's Path, Ginkaku-ji to Nanzen-ji
adventure.description: Two kilometres of canal-side stone path under cherry trees, named for the professor who walked it to work and thought about nothing else.
adventure.bonus: Walk the whole length without taking your phone out once.

adventure.title: Climb Iwatayama to the Monkeys Above Arashiyama
adventure.description: A steep twenty-minute switchback up from the river to a hilltop where a hundred and twenty wild macaques live and the whole city sits behind them.
adventure.bonus: Buy the feed and hand it over from inside the hut, exactly as instructed.

adventure.title: Sanzen-in and the Moss Floor at Ohara
adventure.description: An hour north of the city into a mountain village where a temple garden's floor is unbroken moss under maples, and the tour buses mostly do not come.
adventure.bonus: Find the small stone jizo figures hidden in the moss. There are more than you will spot first time.

adventure.title: Throw a Clay Disc Off the Cliff at Jingo-ji
adventure.description: A mountain temple above the Kiyotaki valley where you buy unglazed clay discs and fling them off a terrace into the gorge to throw away your misfortune.
adventure.bonus: Throw one for something you have actually been carrying around, not a joke.

adventure.title: Tofuku-ji's Maple Valley from the Tsutenkyo Bridge
adventure.description: A covered wooden bridge spanning a ravine packed with two thousand maples, plus the best modern Zen gardens in the city behind it.
adventure.bonus: Do the four gardens of the Hojo first, while everyone else is queueing for the bridge.

adventure.title: Ride Out to Uji Along the River
adventure.description: Half an hour south to the town that has grown Japan's best green tea for eight hundred years, with a phoenix-roofed temple from the year 1053 on the bank.
adventure.bonus: Find the Byodo-in's facade on a ten-yen coin while standing in front of the real thing.

adventure.title: Cable Car and Funicular Up Mount Hiei
adventure.description: Two linked mountain railways from the north of the city to a 1,200-year-old temple complex strung along a ridge above Lake Biwa.
adventure.bonus: Stay on the ridge long enough to see the lake on one side and Kyoto on the other.

adventure.title: The Sagano Romantic Train with the Sides Open
adventure.description: An old sightseeing railway along the Hozu gorge where you book the open-sided carriage and hang out over the river the whole way.
adventure.bonus: Ride the open car even in the cold, and sit on the river side.

adventure.title: Climb the Fushimi Inari Torii to the Summit
adventure.description: Ten thousand vermilion gates climbing a wooded mountain, and almost nobody goes past the first twenty minutes to the shrine at the top.
adventure.bonus: Read the donor's name carved on the back of a gate somewhere above the halfway point.

adventure.title: Hike Over the Mountain from Kurama to Kibune
adventure.description: A two-hour climb through cedar roots and mountain temples from one village to the next, ending at a river gorge lined with wooden inns.
adventure.bonus: Walk the stretch where the tree roots cover the whole path without touching the handrail.

adventure.title: Kiyomizu-dera's Veranda and the Otowa Waterfall
adventure.description: A wooden stage held forty feet above the hillside on timber columns and no nails, with three streams of spring water to drink from underneath it.
adventure.bonus: Pick only one of the three streams and commit to whatever it grants.

adventure.title: The Arashiyama Bamboo Grove at First Light
adventure.description: A corridor of bamboo fifty feet high that is shoulder-to-shoulder by nine in the morning and completely empty at six.
adventure.bonus: Stand still with your eyes shut and listen to the stalks knocking together.

adventure.title: Daimonji-yama, the Hill with the Burning Character
adventure.description: An hour's climb from behind Ginkaku-ji up to the giant kanji that gets set alight every August, with the entire city grid laid out below it.
adventure.bonus: Stand inside one of the stone fire beds that forms the character's strokes.

adventure.title: The Hozugawa River Boat Through the Gorge
adventure.description: Two hours in a flat-bottomed wooden boat poled and rowed sixteen kilometres down a canyon from Kameoka, finishing at Arashiyama.
adventure.bonus: Buy something off the snack boat that pulls alongside near the end.

adventure.title: Cycle the Kamo River End to End
adventure.description: A flat riverside path with no traffic on it, running the length of the city past herons, buskers and students sitting in a row on the bank.
adventure.bonus: Ride as far north as the delta where the two rivers meet, then cross on the stepping stones.
